hints: For each value in b you only need a yes/no answer: does it exist in a? Which structure answers that in O(1)?
Put a in a hash set. Collect values of b that are in it into a second set (so duplicates count once), then sort what you collected.

1. Put every value of a into set seen.
  2. For each value of b that is in seen, add it to set common.
  3. Copy common into a list and sort it.
  4. Return the list (it is empty when nothing is shared).

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For each value of b, scan the whole of a, and skip values already collected.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Sort both arrays and walk them with two pointers, skipping duplicates.
approaches.time: O(N log N + M log M)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Hash set of a, collect matches into a set, then sort only the matches.
approaches.time: O(N + M + K log K), K = number of common values

explain: For a = [1, 2, 2, 1] and b = [2, 2], the set of a is {1, 2}. Both 2s from b are in it, but the common set keeps only one 2, so we return [2]. In the second sample nothing from [2, 4] is in {1, 3, 5}, so we return an empty list. A TreeSet in Java would keep the matches sorted automatically; sorting a small list at the end works just as well.
recognize: "Values present in both lists, each once" → set lookup for membership, a set for uniqueness.
